A wave of investor enthusiasm for enterprise artificial intelligence workflow tools sent Appian (NASDAQ:APPN) soaring 24.2% this week.

Appian stock changed hands at $52.35 as of the close on Friday, Oct. 23, up 27.2% this week from Friday, Oct. 16's close, according to data provided by S&P Global Market Intelligence. Over the same period, the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) fell 0.5%, and the Nasdaq-100 fell 0.7%.

Image source: Getty Images.

AI agent controls and pre-earnings momentum drive the rally

Appian released product updates showcasing tools that give enterprise customers tighter control over automated AI agents, helping businesses run processes safely. The product news coincided with broader sector coverage highlighting Appian's strong operational momentum following its second-quarter performance, where the company generated $203.3 million in revenue--up 19.1% year over year--and delivered an elevated full-year outlook.

Appian sells low-code software that allows businesses to build automated workflows and integrate artificial intelligence agents into their operations. Its platform connects data across disparate corporate systems, enabling enterprise clients, including financial institutions and government agencies, to automate complex operational tasks.

Appian trades at a price-to-sales (P/S) ratio of 4.9. The company generated $203.3 million in its last reported quarter ending June 30, 2026, but posted a net loss of $11.8 million, underscoring its ongoing push toward sustained profitability. This week's momentum shifts the near-term focus to whether Appian can convert its new enterprise AI features into accelerated subscription growth.

What to watch next for Appian

Investors will not have to wait long for an operational checkup. Appian plans to release its third-quarter 2026 financial results before the market opens on Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026.

Key items to watch include acceleration in subscription revenue and progress toward GAAP profitability. As of June 30, 2026, Appian held $167.9 million in cash and short-term investments against $295.3 million in total debt, including lease obligations, making consistent cash flow generation an important long-term milestone.

Is Appian stock a buy?

While Appian stock powered higher this week, those who have had it on their radars shouldn't feel that the recent rise means that shares are too pricey to consider. Trading at 4.9 sales, Appian stock is priced at a slight premium to its five-year average P/S of 4.6 -- hardly a valuation that should preclude growth investors from clicking the buy button.

title: Why Hasbro Stock Surged This Week
detail:
Why Hasbro Stock Surged This Week
Howard Smith, The Motley Fool
Sat, October 24, 2026 at 12:33 PM EDT 4 min read
HAS
^GSPC
Trade Hasbro on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

A blowout third-quarter earnings report driven by record card-game sales sent Hasbro (NASDAQ:HAS) surging 18.9% this week.

Hasbro stock changed hands at $117.44 as of the close on Friday, Oct. 23, up 18.9% from Friday, Oct. 16's close. Across those five sessions, the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) was down 0.5%, and the Nasdaq-100 was down 0.8%.

Magic: The Gathering and guidance expansion drive the rally

Hasbro delivered a strong third quarter, posting revenue of $1.60 billion, up 15% year over year beating consensus estimates of $1.48 billion. Adjusted earnings per share (EPS) hit $2.90, comfortably beating the $1.86 Wall Street expectation. Robust operating cash flow of $907.3 million through nine months prompted management to double its annual share repurchase goal from $200 million to $400 million.

Hasbro designs, manufactures, and licenses play assets, tabletop games, and digital entertainment, selling globally to mass-market retailers, specialty hobby shops, and digital platforms. The company owns major brands like Monopoly and Transformers, but tabletop card franchise Magic: The Gathering served as the main engine this quarter. Magic revenue jumped 34% year over year to exceed $600 million for the first time, while tabletop gaming sales grew sharply.

High-margin licensing and cost discipline added extra momentum, contributing $105 million in savings through the first nine months toward a $150 million annual goal. This week's guidance raise confirms that high-margin digital and tabletop gaming licenses are successfully shifting Hasbro's profit engine away from lower-margin traditional toy manufacturing.

Image source: Getty Images.

What's next for Hasbro

Hasbro trades at a trailing price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 17.3, reflecting investor optimism around expanding profitability. Management raised its full-year constant-currency revenue growth target from a midpoint of 6% to a new range of 7%-9%, and increased operating margin expectations.

Looking ahead, investors will watch how the holiday shopping season impacts traditional consumer toy sales. Management noted that fourth-quarter Magic revenue could dip in the low- to mid-single-digit range due to product release timing. However, two major digital video game launches remain slated for 2027. Hasbro expects to report its next quarterly earnings in early February 2027.

Is Hasbro Stock a Buy?

While a P/E of about 17 doesn't seem excessive, it does represent the highest level for Hasbro stock in the last year. That's because the company is firing on all cylinders. Magic: The Gathering revenue surged 34% year over year in Q3, breaking last quarter's record. The company also plans to launch two more digital games in 2027, Exodus and Warlock.

__Now Live: Discover how much upside your favorite stocks could have using TIKR's new Valuation Model (It's free)__ >>>

What Happened?

DoorDash (DASH) fell 3.53% to $179.38 on October 23 after The Information reported that Instacart (CART) is exploring a sale and has held preliminary talks with DoorDash and Uber (UBER). Instacart closed about 9% higher and Uber about 3% lower, according to Reuters, while the S&P 500 slipped 0.43%. The split suggests investors were pricing what a deal could cost a buyer.

After the close, Bloomberg reported that Uber had walked away from talks with Instacart, citing one person familiar with the matter. If that holds, DoorDash is the only buyer named in the reports still in discussions. DoorDash is down 20.8% in 2026 and 33.3% below its $269.00 52-week high.

DoorDash Drawdowns (TIKR)
What $16 Billion Would Buy That DoorDash Doesn't Already Have

The Information estimated that a typical 30% to 40% takeover premium would value Instacart at roughly $16 billion to $17 billion, per Reuters. Spread across DoorDash's 433.30 million shares, that is about $37 to $39 a share, or roughly a fifth of its $77.72 billion market cap. It is also about eight times the $2.04 billion of net cash DoorDash reported at its latest quarter. No terms have been reported.

DoorDash would not be buying its way into grocery. It said in February that it became the top U.S. third-party marketplace by order count across grocery, convenience, alcohol, and retail in 2025, based on YipitData. That ranking counts orders, not dollars, and Reuters pointed to Instacart's established marketplace and retailer ties as the prize for a buyer.

Antitrust is the main hurdle. DoorDash discussed buying Instacart in 2021 at a reported $40 billion to $50 billion valuation, and those talks fell apart partly over regulatory concerns, according to The Information. The current talks may not produce a deal, and none of the three companies commented.

DoorDash's Own Grocery Fix Is Already Running

On the August 5 earnings call, Co-Founder, Chair and CEO Tony Xu said "grocers don't know their inventory," so customers can pay a delivery premium and still not get what they ordered.

DoorDash's answer is DashMart Fulfillment Services, warehouses it runs near 24/7 for partner retailers. DoorDash is "seeing 10 times better error rates because we're running the inventory," he said, and he estimated it delivers roughly one-tenth of the retail and grocery selection available in most cities.

CFO Ravi Inukonda said new verticals should turn gross profit positive: "We're on track for that in the second half of the year." That remains a management target, and Xu called the warehouse build "complicated."

Here are five you should consider right now: Hormel (NYSE: HRL), Clorox (NYSE: CLX), Realty Income (NYSE: O), Enbridge (NYSE: ENB), and Enterprise Products Partners (NYSE: EPD).

Consumer staples companies are feeling the pinch

Rising inflation has led consumers to tighten their budgets. At the same time, inflation has left consumer staples companies with elevated costs, putting pressure on margins. And consumer buying habits are shifting toward healthier products. Hormel and Clorox are both working through this rough patch as best they can, but Wall Street is in a show-me mood. detail:
The Puzzle Pieces for a Stock Market Crash Are Taking Shape, With 4 Historically Flawless Indicators Now Sounding the Alarm
Sean Williams, The Motley Fool

^GSPC

Roughly two weeks ago, the stock market celebrated the fourth anniversary of the current bull market. Since the end of the 2022 bear market, the benchmark S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) and tech-driven Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX:^IXIC) have more than doubled, while the iconic Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJINDICES:^DJI) has rallied an impressive 84%.

Though several catalysts have fueled this rally, including record S&P 500 share buybacks and better-than-expected corporate earnings, the artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure build-out takes the cake. The otherworldly amount of capital being spent on the AI data center build-out is boosting short- and long-term growth projections.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

At the same time, bull markets don't last indefinitely.

Image source: Getty Images.

The puzzle pieces for a stock market crash and/or bear market are falling into place, with four historically flawless indicators now sounding the alarm.

This is the second-priciest stock market in history

Perhaps the most front-and-center issue for Wall Street's AI-driven bull market is that it's historically pricey.

On the one hand, value is one of the trickiest subjects to tackle. Given that there's no one-size-fits-all way to evaluate and value individual companies or the broader market, subjectivity and emotion often come into play. These variables make it virtually impossible to accurately predict short-term directional moves in the Dow Jones Industrial Average, S&P 500, and Nasdaq Composite.

On the other hand, the S&P 500's Shiller Price-to-Earnings (P/E) Ratio, also known as the Cyclically Adjusted P/E Ratio (CAPE Ratio), has demonstrated the ability to push past investors' emotions and subjectivity and provide apples-to-apples valuation comparisons for the broader market, dating back to the early 1870s.

When backtested over 156 years, the Shiller P/E Ratio has averaged 17.44. As of the closing bell on Oct. 21, the Shiller P/E topped 41, marking the second-priciest stock market in history.

Since January 1871, the CAPE Ratio has exceeded 30 during a continuous bull market only six times, including the present. The previous five instances were all eventually (keyword!) followed by declines of 20% to 89% in one or more of Wall Street's major stock indexes.

title: I'd Put Most of a Lump Sum Into an S&P 500 Fund Right Away. Here's When I Wouldn't.
detail:
I'd Put Most of a Lump Sum Into an S&P 500 Fund Right Away. Here's When I Wouldn't.
Daniel Sparks, The Motley Fool
Sat, October 24, 2026 at 8:12 AM EDT 5 min read
^GSPC
NVDA
Trade NVIDIA on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

The S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) set its latest record close, 7,818.93, on Oct. 6. As of this writing, it's just a little over 1% under that mark. For anyone with a lot of cash meant for an index fund, putting it all in so close to a record can seem like asking for bad timing.

The common alternative is dollar-cost averaging, which here means splitting the money into equal chunks and buying over several months. Vanguard tested the two methods in a 2012 study and found investing all at once did better around two-thirds of the time.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

I ran a simpler check of my own going back to 1950 and got a similar result. So I'd lean toward putting most of the money in right away. But spreading purchases out still has a use, and it shows up in the bad years.

Image source: Getty Images.

What Vanguard found

Vanguard's study, called "Dollar-cost averaging just means taking risk later," compared both approaches over rolling 10-year spans in the U.S., the U.K., and Australia. The U.S. data covered 1926 through 2011, and the two other markets had shorter histories. In the main version, the waiting money was in cash investments and went into a mix of 60% stocks and 40% bonds over 12 months. Investing all at once won 67% of the U.S. periods, and the U.K. and Australia were at 67% and 66%. On average, the lump sum ended around 2.3% ahead in the U.S.

And the longer the money was spread out, the worse it did. Versus a 36-month plan, the lump sum won around 90% of the U.S. periods. The main reason is stocks and bonds have earned more than cash over time, so waiting money tends to buy in at higher prices.

Of course, the study was about a sum already on hand. Vanguard sees investing a piece of every paycheck as a separate case, since that money only comes a little at a time.

What about buying near a record?

Vanguard's main test mixed stocks and bonds, so I ran a stock-only version on the S&P 500. Using month-end closes since 1950, I compared investing a sum all at once to 12 equal monthly purchases. I valued each a year after the first buy, on price alone (without dividends), with the waiting cash earning zero.

Buying all at once won in 651 of the 909 rolling 12-month stretches, or around 72% of the time.

After all, the index itself gained in about three out of four of those stretches. Over the long run, stock prices have tended to follow company earnings higher.

What Flex Bulls Got Right

If you had focused only on headlines about Flex joining the S&P 500 or spinning off its cloud and power unit, it might be easy to forget what actually showed up in your brokerage account. Holding Flex from the start of the year would have returned 20.2%, including dividends. If that outcome depended on investors correctly reading early signals about AI data center demand and outsourcing trends, how confident can you be about the next big announcement?

Narratives are how investors here put a case on the record, with explicit assumptions about revenue, margins and the multiple. Those assumptions imply an estimated Fair Value.

Flex is not the only name tied to this theme. Zero in on 55 AI infrastructure stocks and compare how each one is priced.

The Two Flex Narratives Investors Had To Weigh

The shares cost US$60.42 at the start of the period, so any investor in Flex had to decide which story about the future sounded more convincing.

The bullish narrative pinned fair value at US$65, or 8% above the start price, hinging on ideas such as multi year IoT and electrification demand reshaping outsourced manufacturing and rewarding Flex's push into higher value digital services.

The bearish narrative set fair value at US$44.27, or 27% below the start price, and worked off more muted assumptions such as 1.0% revenue growth, a 3.0% profit margin and a 25.0x future P/E over a 10 year horizon.

NasdaqGS:FLEX Trailing 12-Month Earnings & Revenue History as at Oct 2026
What The Flex Evidence Actually Tested

The clearest business signal came from Flex's Q1 2027 report, where revenue reached US$7,928m and net income was US$285m, with net margin at 3.6%. That combination leaned toward the bullish case that talked about higher profitability, although the margin level still sat close enough to the bearish 3.0% assumption that the question was not settled.

The key lesson here is to pin narratives to one or two hard levers. For a company like Flex, that means tracking both the reported net margin and any segment separation plans, and then checking whether each new quarter moves those numbers toward the thesis you believed on day one.

What Flex's Current Price Already Assumes

Flex now trades at US$76.55, after a 20.2% gain from the start of the year, while the selected Narrative's Fair Value still sits above that level based on its own assumptions.

The Narrative leans on AI infrastructure programs, the Axiom spin and factory automation, and argues today's price still does not fully credit sustained high value orders displacing weaker legacy work.

"The main thing that has to go right is that Flex and Axiom convert the AI-driven power and data center build-out, including the EPC Power acquisition and expanded AI hardware programs, into sustained orders that more than offset pressure in legacy consumer and lower-value revenue streams."
